Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Topps Meat Co. on Saturday expanded a recall of ground beef from about 300,000  pounds to 21.7 million pounds, one of the largest meat recalls in U.S. history. The recalled products are all ground beef patties with various brand names. In a statement, the Elizabeth, New Jersey, company said the hamburger patties may be contaminated with E. coli O157:H7, a bacterium that can cause severe diarrhea and cramps, as well as other complications. A statement from the U.S. Department of Agriculture said 25 illnesses are under investigation in Connecticut, Florida, Indiana, Maine, New Jersey, New York, Ohio and Pennsylvania. The ground beef products being recalled have a "sell by date" or a "best if used by date" between September 25, 2007, and September 25, 2008, Topps' statement said.  Watch the latest on the beef recall » . The packages also have the marking "Est. 9748" inside the USDA mark of inspection. Tuesday, the company announced a recall of about 331,000 pounds of hamburger meat, according to the USDA. "Because the health and safety of our consumers is our top priority, we are taking these expansive measures," said Vice President of Operations Geoffrey Livermore in the statement. "Topps is continuing to work with the USDA, state departments of health, retailers and distributors to ensure the safety of our consumers. Additionally, we have augmented our internal quality control procedures with microbiologists and food safety experts. We sincerely regret any inconvenience and concerns this may cause our consumers," Livermore said. This is the company's first recall in its 65 years of business, the statement said. Consumers who find the products at home are asked to cut off the UPC code and return it to Topps for a full refund, then dispose of the product immediately, Topps spokeswoman Michelle Williams said. The company said to avoid E. coli, consumers should wash hands thoroughly after handling the beef. Topps set up a toll-free recall help line at (888) 734-0451. Williams said because the products may have been produced up to a year ago, many of them have already been safely consumed. Production in the ground beef area of the company's plant in Elizabeth has been shut down until all the investigations are complete, Williams said in a phone interview. "We're working with the USDA and the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and conducting our own investigation," she added. The products, all ground beef patties and hamburgers with various brand names, were distributed mainly in the northeastern United States, but went to retailers in many other areas of the country as well, Williams said. While the sheer size of the recall is large, two other companies have been involved in larger recalls. In 2002, Pilgrim's Pride recalled more than 27 million pounds of poultry, and Hudson Foods recalled 25 million pounds of ground beef in 1997. E-mail to a friend .

# Major Ground Beef Recall Announced Amid E. Coli Contamination Fears

**Nearly 16,000 Pounds of Product Pulled from Shelves Across Multiple States**

A large meat processing company has issued an urgent recall of ground beef products after routine testing revealed potential contamination with E. coli O157:H7, a dangerous strain of bacteria that can cause severe illness, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS).

The recall affects approximately 15,800 pounds of ground beef products distributed to grocery stores and wholesalers across several states, with products bearing "sell by" dates that have not yet expired, raising concerns that contaminated meat may still be in consumers' refrigerators and freezers.

## Details of the Recall

According to the USDA, the affected products include various weights of ground beef packaged in plastic-wrapped trays, sold under multiple label names at retail locations. Each package bears an establishment number "EST. 2879" inside the USDA mark of inspection, which consumers can use to verify whether their purchased products are subject to the recall.

FSIS officials say the issue was discovered during routine sampling as part of the agency's ongoing food safety verification testing program, which regularly screens meat products for pathogens before and after they reach store shelves.

"The problem was identified through our standard testing protocols, and once confirmed, the establishment was notified immediately," an FSIS spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working closely with the company to ensure all affected product is removed from commerce."

## Health Risks

E. coli O157:H7 is a particularly dangerous strain of the bacteria that can cause bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal cramps, and vomiting. In vulnerable populations—including young children, the elderly, and individuals with compromised immune systems—the infection can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a serious condition that can result in kidney failure.

Symptoms typically appear within three to four days after exposure, though the incubation period can range from one to ten days. Health officials are urging anyone who has consumed the recalled product and is experiencing symptoms to seek medical attention immediately and inform their healthcare provider of possible E. coli exposure.

As of this report, no confirmed illnesses have been directly linked to the recalled products, though FSIS noted that investigations are ongoing and the agency will update the public if that changes.

## Company Response

In a statement released Tuesday, the company said it was cooperating fully with federal regulators and had voluntarily initiated the recall "out of an abundance of caution for our customers' safety."

"We take food safety extremely seriously and hold ourselves to the highest standards," the company said. "As soon as we were made aware of the potential contamination, we acted swiftly to identify all affected lots and notify our distribution partners. We deeply regret any concern this may cause our customers."

The company added that it is conducting an internal investigation to determine the source of the contamination and is reviewing its safety protocols to prevent future incidents.

## What Consumers Should Do

The USDA is advising anyone who purchased the recalled ground beef to not consume it. Instead, consumers should either throw the product away or return it to the place of purchase for a refund.

Because ground beef is often frozen for later use, officials are especially concerned that some contaminated product may still be sitting in home freezers, potentially months after purchase.

Consumers are urged to check their freezers and refrigerators against the list of recalled products, which includes specific lot numbers and package codes available on the FSIS website.

Retailers who received the affected shipments have been notified and are in the process of removing the product from shelves.

## Ongoing Investigation

FSIS said it will continue to monitor the situation and work with public health partners at the state and local level to track any potential illnesses linked to the recalled beef.

The agency emphasized that home food safety practices remain critical regardless of recalls, reminding the public that ground beef should always be cooked to an internal temperature of 160 degrees Fahrenheit, as measured by a food thermometer, to kill harmful bacteria.

This is a developing story, and CNN will provide updates as more information becomes available from federal health officials and the company involved.

*For a complete list of recalled products, including specific UPC codes and sell-by dates, consumers can visit the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service website or contact the company's consumer hotline directly.*

---

*Note: This article is a fictional/illustrative example created for demonstration purposes and does not describe an actual recall event.*

**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**

Topps Meat Company has dramatically expanded its recall of frozen ground beef products, now totaling approximately 21.7 million pounds, following continued reports of E. coli O157:H7 contamination linked to the products. This marks one of the largest beef recalls in U.S. history.

- Vomiting

# Topps Meat Co. Recall Expands to 21.7 Million Pounds Amid E. Coli Contamination Fears

**Federal officials warn consumers as ground beef recall balloons more than 70-fold in one of the largest meat recalls in U.S. history**

What began as a modest recall of 300,000 pounds of frozen ground beef patties has exploded into a massive 21.7 million-pound recall, as Topps Meat Company scrambles to contain the fallout from E. coli contamination concerns that have alarmed food safety officials and consumers nationwide.

## From Small Recall to Major Crisis

The recall, initially announced as a precautionary measure affecting a limited batch of products, has grown dramatically after further investigation by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) revealed the scope of potential contamination was far more extensive than first believed. The company, based in Elizabeth, New Jersey, has been forced to pull nearly two years' worth of production from store shelves and freezers across the country.

Topps Meat Co., a major supplier of frozen hamburger patties sold under various brand names to grocery stores and retailers nationwide, expanded the recall after health officials linked several illnesses to products traced back to the company's processing facility.

## Health Concerns Mount

E. coli O157:H7, the strain of bacteria at the center of the recall, can cause severe symptoms including bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and in serious cases, kidney failure — particularly dangerous for children, the elderly, and those with weakened immune systems. Several cases of illness across multiple states have been linked to the contaminated beef, prompting the aggressive expansion of the recall.

Health officials are urging consumers who may have purchased frozen ground beef patties from Topps to check their freezers immediately, discard any recalled products, and monitor for symptoms of E. coli infection, which typically appear within two to five days of exposure.

## Massive Scope of Recalled Products

The scale of the recall — encompassing production spanning nearly two years — has raised serious questions about the company's quality control processes and the adequacy of federal meat inspection protocols. Products affected include various package sizes and brand labels distributed to supermarkets, big-box retailers, and food service distributors across the country.

Consumers are advised to check for specific establishment numbers and use-by dates printed on packaging, and to consult the USDA's website or hotline for a complete list of affected products.

## Industry and Regulatory Fallout

The dramatic escalation from 300,000 to 21.7 million pounds has drawn sharp criticism from consumer advocacy groups, who argue the incident underscores systemic weaknesses in the nation's meat inspection system. Critics point to the initial underestimation of the recall's scope as evidence that current testing and traceability measures fail to adequately protect public health.

Food safety experts note that ground beef is particularly susceptible to E. coli contamination because the grinding process can mix bacteria from the surface of meat throughout the entire product, unlike whole cuts where contamination typically remains on the exterior and can be eliminated through proper cooking.

The USDA has faced pressure to explain how the recall grew so dramatically and whether earlier, more decisive action could have prevented additional consumer exposure.

## Company Response

Topps Meat Co. has stated it is fully cooperating with federal investigators and has ceased production while conducting a comprehensive internal review of its safety protocols. Company officials expressed regret over the incident and emphasized their commitment to consumer safety, though the massive scope of the recall has raised questions about the long-term viability of the company's operations.

## What Consumers Should Do

Federal health officials are advising anyone who has purchased frozen ground beef patties in recent months to:

- Check product packaging against the official USDA recall list
- Discard or return any recalled products immediately
- Avoid tasting suspect products, even briefly, as a way of checking safety
- Thoroughly clean any surfaces, utensils, or containers that may have come into contact with recalled products
- Seek medical attention if experiencing symptoms of foodborne illness after consuming potentially affected beef

The FSIS continues to investigate the source of contamination and is working with Topps Meat Co. to ensure all affected products are removed from the marketplace. Additional updates are expected as the investigation continues.

*This is a developing story. Consumers are encouraged to check the USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service website for the most current recall information.*

# Major Poultry Producer Recalls 8.5 Million Pounds of Chicken Products Over Listeria Concerns

**CHICAGO (AP)** — Heartland Fresh Foods issued a sweeping recall Tuesday of approximately 8.5 million pounds of ready-to-eat chicken products after routine testing revealed potential contamination with *Listeria monocytogenes*, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service announced.

The recall affects 47 product varieties, including pre-packaged chicken strips, diced chicken breast, and rotisserie-style chicken products distributed to retailers in 23 states between March 15 and April 28. The affected items carry establishment number P-4471 and were sold under the Heartland Fresh and several private-label store brands.

The USDA said the contamination was discovered during a routine sampling program at the company's Springfield, Missouri, processing facility. No illnesses had been confirmed as of Tuesday afternoon, though health officials are investigating several reports of gastrointestinal illness that may be linked to the products.

"We are taking this action out of an abundance of caution and in full cooperation with USDA officials," said Marcus Chen, Heartland Fresh's chief executive officer, in a statement released alongside the recall notice. "Food safety is not negotiable at our company, and we will not rest until we fully understand how this occurred and ensure it cannot happen again."

Chen said the company has voluntarily suspended production at the Springfield facility pending a full investigation and has engaged an independent food safety auditing firm to review its sanitation protocols.

Sandra Williams, Heartland Fresh's vice president of quality assurance, said the company's internal testing caught the issue before it could become "significantly worse," though she acknowledged the scale of the recall was troubling.

"When you're dealing with a pathogen like *Listeria*, which can survive refrigeration and has a longer incubation period than something like salmonella, you have to act decisively and communicate clearly with consumers," Williams said in a call with reporters Tuesday. "We understand the anxiety this creates for families, and we're working around the clock with retailers to ensure these products come off shelves immediately."

## Comparisons to Past Outbreaks

The recall is among the largest poultry-related recalls in the past five years, though it falls short of the 2021 recall by Aspen Valley Foods, which pulled 12 million pounds of ground turkey products after a salmonella outbreak sickened more than 350 people across 42 states and was linked to one death.

Food safety experts noted similarities to the 2019 listeria scare involving Sunnydale Provisions, which recalled 6.9 million pounds of deli meats. That incident, which health officials eventually linked to eight deaths and dozens of hospitalizations, prompted the USDA to expand its environmental sampling requirements for ready-to-eat meat facilities — the same protocols that flagged Tuesday's contamination at Heartland Fresh.

"This recall shows the system working as intended, in some ways," said Dr. Elena Rodriguez, a food safety epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota who was not involved in the investigation. "Compare this to a decade ago, when contamination often wasn't caught until people were already getting sick. The expanded testing requirements implemented after the Sunnydale outbreak are exactly why this was identified at the plant level."

Rodriguez cautioned, however, that the scale of the current recall — the third-largest listeria-related poultry recall since 2015, according to USDA data — underscores persistent challenges in large-scale food processing sanitation.

## Consumer Guidance

The USDA has published a full list of affected products, lot numbers, and "use by" dates on its website. Consumers who purchased the recalled items are urged not to eat them and either discard them or return them to the place of purchase for a full refund.

Listeria infection, or listeriosis, can cause fever, muscle aches, and gastrointestinal symptoms, and poses particular risk to pregnant women, adults over 65, and individuals with weakened immune systems. In severe cases, the infection can spread to the nervous system, causing headaches, stiff neck, confusion, and loss of balance.

Chen said Heartland Fresh has established a dedicated hotline and email address for consumers with questions about the recall and is offering full refunds regardless of proof of purchase.

"We know trust is earned, and right now we have work to do to earn it back," Chen said. "But we are committed to transparency throughout this process."

The FSIS said it will continue monitoring the investigation and will update the public if additional products are identified. The agency's Springfield district office is conducting an on-site review of Heartland Fresh's manufacturing practices this week.

---

*This story will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# 2007 U.S. Meat Recall: E. coli O157:H7 Contamination

## Overview

2007 was a notably severe year for E. coli-related meat recalls in the United States, with the Topps Meat Company recall standing as one of the most significant food safety incidents of the decade. This report examines the major recall event, the company's response, associated health warnings, and historical context.

## The Topps Meat Company Recall

### Background
In late September 2007, Topps Meat Company, LLC, based in Elizabeth, New Jersey, initiated what became one of the largest beef recalls in U.S. history. The company had been in operation for approximately 67 years, producing frozen hamburger patties sold under brand names including Topps, Blue Ridge Farms, and various store brands for supermarket chains.

### Scope of the Recall
- **Initial recall (September 25, 2007):** Approximately 331,000 pounds of frozen ground beef patties
- **Expanded recall (September 29, 2007):** The recall grew dramatically to approximately **21.7 million pounds** of frozen ground beef products
- Products had been distributed nationwide and were traced back to production dates spanning several months

### Cause of Contamination
Investigators from the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) linked the contamination to E. coli O157:H7, a particularly dangerous strain of the bacteria. Investigation suggested the contamination may have originated from raw materials, though the exact source in the supply chain remained difficult to pinpoint precisely—a common challenge in ground beef contamination cases due to the mixing of meat from multiple animals and sources during processing.

## Health Impact and Warnings

### Reported Illnesses
The outbreak was linked to at least **40 confirmed illnesses** across multiple states, including:
- New York
- New Jersey
- Pennsylvania
- Connecticut
- Florida
- Maine
- Ohio

Several victims required hospitalization, and some cases involved hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a severe complication that can cause kidney failure, particularly dangerous in children and elderly individuals.

### Public Health Warnings
The USDA and CDC issued warnings emphasizing:
- Consumers should not eat recalled products, even if previously frozen
- Ground beef should be cooked to an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C)
- Use of a meat thermometer was strongly recommended, as color alone is not a reliable indicator of doneness
- Cross-contamination prevention in kitchens handling raw ground beef

## Company Response

### Topps Meat Company's Actions
The company's response, while cooperative with federal investigators, ultimately proved insufficient to save the business:

1. **Recall cooperation:** Topps worked with FSIS to identify affected lot codes and distribution channels
2. **Production halt:** The company ceased all ground beef production
3. **Business closure:** On October 5, 2007—just days after the expanded recall—Topps Meat Company announced it was **ceasing operations permanently**, laying off approximately 87 employees
4. **Statement:** Company officials cited the financial impossibility of surviving such a large-scale recall, given the company's size and the scope of the contamination

The rapid collapse of Topps illustrated how devastating a major recall could be for a mid-sized food company, essentially ending the business within two weeks of the initial recall announcement.

## Regulatory and Industry Aftermath

### FSIS Response
The incident prompted the USDA to:
- Review inspection protocols for ground beef processors
- Increase scrutiny of testing procedures for E. coli O157:H7
- Examine the adequacy of "test and hold" procedures, which some critics argued Topps had not adequately implemented

### Criticism and Policy Discussion
The Topps case reignited debates about:
- Whether ground beef producers should be required to hold products until pathogen testing is complete
- The adequacy of USDA's regulatory authority over meat safety
- Supply chain transparency and traceability requirements

## Historical Context: Pattern of E. coli Recalls

The Topps recall did not occur in isolation but fit into a troubling pattern of E. coli contamination events:

### Jack in the Box Outbreak (1993)
Often considered the watershed moment for E. coli awareness in the U.S., this outbreak sickened over 700 people and caused four deaths, primarily among children. It led to significant changes in food safety regulation, including the USDA's adoption of the Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) system.

### ConAgra Beef Recalls (2002)
ConAgra recalled approximately 19 million pounds of ground beef due to E. coli O157:H7 contamination—at the time, one of the largest beef recalls in history.

### 2007 as a Peak Year
Beyond Topps, 2007 saw multiple other E. coli-related beef recalls, including:
- United Food Group recall (over 5.7 million pounds)
- Various smaller regional recalls

The concentration of incidents in 2007 led some food safety advocates to describe it as a "wake-up call" year, prompting renewed calls for regulatory reform.

### Subsequent Regulatory Changes
Following 2007's recalls, USDA/FSIS took steps including:
- Declaring additional E. coli serotypes ("Big Six" non-O157 STECs) as adulterants in 2011
- Enhanced testing requirements
- Continued refinement of HACCP verification procedures

## Conclusion

The 2007 Topps Meat Company recall represents a pivotal case study in American food safety history—demonstrating both the severe public health risks posed by E. coli O157:H7 contamination and the significant economic consequences recalls can have on food producers. The incident contributed to ongoing regulatory evolution in meat safety oversight and remains referenced in food safety literature as an example of how quickly contamination issues can escalate from initial detection to company-ending crisis.

---

*Note: This report is compiled from general knowledge of this historical event. For precise statistics, official reports, and complete case details, readers should consult primary sources including FSIS recall notices, CDC outbreak investigation reports, and contemporary news coverage from 2007.*
